1:
Adam Clarke gives the chapter its shape in a sentence: an exhortation to acquire wisdom in order to be preserved from impure connections, then the character of a harlot and her conduct towards a youth who fell into her snare, then solemn exhortations to avoid the evil. Matthew Henry notices that this opening repeats one earlier in the book and ends where that one ended, at the strange woman, the only difference being that the earlier passage said keep thy father’s commandment and this one says keep mine, which comes all to one since the teacher speaks to us as to sons.

The binding on the fingers draws four different pictures and one piece of ritual. Charles Ellicott supplies the ritual: the thong of the phylactery for the left arm was wound seven times round the arm and as many times round the middle finger. John Gill offers three figures without choosing — the words as ready as if at the fingers’ ends, a thread tied round a finger as a reminder, or rings at once memorial and ornamental — and then a fourth, that the fingers being instruments of action the command is to put the teaching into practice. Henry keeps to jewellery, a diamond ring, a signet on the right hand, a wedding ring worn as the badge of espousal to God. John Wesley reduces it to a ring continually in a man’s eye.

On keeping the law as the apple of the eye, Clarke is anatomical, the pupil being of such essential necessity to sight and so easily injured; Henry turns the same fact into an argument, that a little thing offends the eye and nature has therefore guarded it well, and adds that those who reproach strict walking as needless preciseness forget that the law in the heart is the eye of the soul. Keil and Delitzsch add the philology, that the Hebrew and the Arabic alike call the pupil the little man of the eye.

Keil and Delitzsch spend most of their space on two textual points. The Greek, they report, carries an extra couplet after the first verse, which here disturbs the connection. And the imperative in the second verse is pointed one way elsewhere and another here, on the authority of a Jewish grammarian and of certain manuscripts and editions, so that it joins a class of forms taking a short vowel under a pausal accent; no reason for this, they say, is to be perceived. At the window they turn lexical: the word is properly a place where the wall is bored through, the lattice comes from a root meaning cool and fresh and keeps off the rays of the sun, and the verb for looking out means primarily to make oneself long in order to see.

The strange woman is read at two levels. Clarke names her flatly, the prostitute, the adulteress. Gill takes her literally and then allegorically, so that the teaching guards not only against fleshly lusts but against the errors, heresies, idolatry, superstition and will worship of Rome, a stranger to God and to true godliness. Henry generalises differently, making her sin itself, that flattering but destroying thing, and asking that the word of God confirm our dread of it, discover its fallacies and supply answers to all its flatteries. Keil and Delitzsch keep her concrete and note that the author proves how necessary wisdom is against such enticements by appealing to something he says he saw himself. Gill takes the sister of the fourth verse for the Gospel and for Christ; Wesley asks only that the reader acquaint and delight himself with her.
6:
Is the story reported or invented? Matthew Henry says it is supposed to be a parable, but doubts it was too true, and still too often true. He explains the window by the office: the teacher was a magistrate who inspected the manners of his subjects and looked through his casement to see with his own eyes those who little thought his eye was upon them, though here he writes rather as a watchman warning of an ambush. Keil and Delitzsch take the same view without argument, the author showing the necessity of wisdom by a reference to his own observation and describing the event as he watched it.

The young man is dissected by Henry, who counts six faults: his youth, since fleshly lusts are called youthful not to excuse but to aggravate them; his want of understanding, having ventured to sea without ballast, pilot or compass; his company, being simple among the simple; his idleness; his gait, the word implying a starched and stately manner, so that he appeared a formal fop whose accomplishment was to dress well and walk with a good air, fit game for that bird of prey; and his hours, since we must take heed not only of idle days but of idle evenings. Charles Ellicott makes the same judgment in six words, that he was not yet vicious, only empty-headed, and notes that the verb of his walking is elsewhere used of the slow step of a religious procession. Adam Clarke renders his folly literally, destitute of a heart, and says he had neither wisdom to discern the evil nor courage to resist the seducer. John Wesley has him idle and careless near the corner where her house stood.

Whether the woman was married divides them. John Gill, Henry and Keil and Delitzsch all take her for a wife: Henry adds that she lived in reputation among her neighbours, and Keil and Delitzsch insist she is no common street-walker but a licentious married wife who, when she wanders abroad, is no better than one. Clarke doubts the marriage: her claim to a husband and a house may have been a falsehood calculated to keep him from thinking he risked anything with a common woman, and he is rather inclined to think it was, since she was subtle of heart. Ellicott glosses her subtlety as feigning love to her husband and devotion to her lovers while caring for neither. Henry’s portrait is the fullest, a woman loud and stubborn, all tongue, impatient of check, who will not bear a yoke, now in the country for the air and now in the streets to see how the market goes; he ends with the line that virtue is a penance to those to whom home is a prison. Clarke adds that sitting in an open place with the face covered was once a harlot’s mark.

The three words for nightfall are read as a progression by all who notice them. Keil and Delitzsch find the designations of time giving the impression of progress to a climax, and defend the first against a critic who denies it means twilight, citing a rabbinic distinction between evening and morning twilight while allowing the root to cover the whole cool half of the day. Ellicott draws the moral: the young man has no excuse of sudden temptation, having trifled with danger from twilight till dark. Gill turns the progression into a timetable of the journey: twilight when he set out, sunset when he had gone a good part of his way, black night when he came near the house. Gill also reads the whole scene twice over, making the simple ones the followers of antichrist, the corner the Popish chapels to be avoided, and the woman the mother of harlots who pretends to be the spouse of Christ, her loudness becoming rebellion against a husband she professes.
14:
Her opening move is religious, and it embarrasses them all. John Gill explains that the peace offerings were eucharistic, most of the victim returning to the offerer to be eaten the same day with friends, so that the invitation is really to supper; he adds that the word can mean a consecrated woman, and calls her a religious harlot. Charles Ellicott stresses that the offering was voluntary and admitted the offerer to feast with God, and draws a parallel his readers would feel: this turning of a religious festival into an occasion for licence is matched by the desecration of the love-feasts at Corinth and by the history of church-feasts nearer home. Adam Clarke goes further, reporting from a book of eastern customs that in many parts of the East the gods are worshipped in brothels and fragments of the offerings divided among the women, and that she insinuates she had vowed for the young man’s safety. Keil and Delitzsch weigh a derivation of the name from holding friendly relationship against one from discharging perfectly, and prefer to call it a thank-payment or due-offering. John Wesley takes the practical point, that she advertises her larder.

The furniture gets more care than the woman. Keil and Delitzsch fix the first noun as the wooden frame, the bed-place rather than the bedding, comparing Arabic words for throne and arbour. Clarke separates two words the English blurs, the couch for meals and the bed to sleep on, takes the tapestry for the covering of the couch, and an old version rendering the next word painted carpets made in Egypt. Ellicott would have coloured or striped coverlets, sets the verse against the extravagance of the women of Jerusalem and the trade of Tyre, and traces myrrh to Arabia and aloes and cinnamon to the east coast of Africa and Ceylon. On the spices Keil and Delitzsch note that the same three names stand together in the Canticles, that the myrrh yields its aroma from resin oozing through the bark in glossy red or golden grains, and that the second name is the Semitic form of an old Indian word for a wood whose scent is in the root. Clarke breaks with them: the word probably does not mean aloes, which is no perfume, but sandal wood.

At the invitation Clarke does something he does nowhere else here. He gives the Hebrew, says his rendering does not half express it and that he forbears, quotes the Latin and the Greek to show they agree, prints the speech from his old manuscript Bible, and concludes that the original is too gross to be literally translated, though quite in character in the mouth of an abandoned woman. Gill compares a poet’s phrase for eyes drunk with love.

Three of them notice the same missing word: she says the man, not my husband. Ellicott notes that she does not even call him her husband; Keil and Delitzsch say she ignores the relation of love and duty she stands in; Gill supposes she avoids it lest it throw a difficulty in the young man’s way or remind herself of her obligation. On the day of his return Ellicott makes the sharpest inference here: the term means the full moon, a fortnight off, so it must now be new moon, when the nights are dark. Keil and Delitzsch render it the same way; Clarke reports the Latin for the full moon and an old version for the day of the assembly, and settles on the approaching festival; Gill takes the money bag as evidence of a long absence. Keil and Delitzsch close by calling what follows the rhetoric of sin, a climax in which she first brings him to yield and then hurries him away, and suspect that the verb used of the husband taking his purse suggested the same verb, turned against him, for her taking of the youth.
21:
All three close readers agree the text here is out of order, and each handles it differently. Keil and Delitzsch say the confusion into which the text has fallen continues here, since the deadly arrow attaches to neither image before it: an ox led to the slaughter is not shot, and a madman put in chains is being rendered harmless, not killed. They report that the Greek solved this by turning the fool into a stag, and refuse the change: no encroachment on the text is needed, only a correct placing of its members, so that the comparison with a bird hurrying to the snare begins a fresh clause. Adam Clarke reports that the two verses have been variously translated and prints a scholar’s corrected version, in which the ox goes to the slaughter, a dog to the chain, a deer runs till the dart strikes his liver, and a bird hastens to the snare; very slight alterations produce these differences, he says, and it is not necessary to pursue them, since all mark the same folly. Charles Ellicott notes that the received sense of the second clause is gained only by transposing the original, and offers the literal alternative, as if in fetters to the place where fools are corrected, which is to say to prison.

On the dart in the liver John Gill gives three reasons at once: it is the fountain of blood and so of life, it is the seat of lust, so that the man is struck where his lust began and where the darts of desire had already wounded him, and the wound may stand for a disease infecting the blood. Clarke keeps to the moral, that all the images mark the stupidity of a man led away by enticing women. John Wesley adds one touch of his own, that the ox goes securely, as if it were going to good pasture. At the verse before, Gill notices that her much fair speech can be rendered her much doctrine, and turns the seduction into false teaching, comparing a woman who called herself a prophetess.

The epilogue is addressed to children in the Hebrew and to a son in three of the versions, as Gill observes. Keil and Delitzsch find a nicety in the verb of straying: it is the word the law of jealousy uses for a wife’s trespass, specially appropriate where a faithless wife has just been drawn. Matthew Henry sets the two roads against each other: never leave the paths of virtue, though strait and narrow, solitary and uphill, for the way of the adulteress, though green and broad and crowded with company; and the command is not merely to keep the feet from those ways but to keep the heart from inclining to them. Gill says the same, that the first motion of the heart is to be checked.

The casualties are counted twice. Gill and Clarke both notice that the words rendered wounded and strong men mean soldiers and mighty men, so that the ruined are not only the weak like the young man of the story but men of riches, wisdom and courage; Clarke adds that many who distinguished themselves in the field and in the cabinet have been destroyed by their mistresses, and that history is full of such examples. Keil and Delitzsch weigh whether the word at the head of the verse means many or great, and decide for many on the strength of places where the two words stand together in that sense. At the last verse Gill notes the noun is plural, ways rather than way, and that the word for the world of the dead often means simply the grave; Clarke takes it through the pit and the grave to the eternal world, and closes with a line about the chambers of death, where pleasure is at an end and illusion mocks no more.
